sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The Umbria-Marche region was thoroughly investigated by means of seismic reflection profiles, and different interpretations of its structural style are available in literature.
The main differences in the interpretations lie in the position of the basal decollement level of the thrusting and of secondary decollement levels. Some researchers (Bally et al., 1986; Doglioni et al., 1994) indicate the bottom of the Triassic evaporites as the basal decollement level and propose that thin-skinned tectonics has characterised the Paleogene-Neogene evolution of the belt. Other researchers (Barchi et al., 1998; Finetti et al., 2001; Lavecchia et al., 2003) consider the upper portion of the magnetic basement involved in thrusting and propose a thick-skinned structural style. In general, there is a good agreement among the researches (Coward et al., 1999; Barchi et al., 1998; Calamita et al., 1994) about the presence of two main decollement levels inside the accretionary prism, the lower one coinciding with the bottom of the Triassic evaporites, on which the major thrust ramps originate, and the shallower one coinciding with the Marne a Fucoidi or Scaglia Cinerea formation, on which minor thrust sheets depart.
Consequently, the regional deformation style is characterised by the presence of deep structures consisting of anticlines involving the Mesozoic-Paleogene carbonate succession, and of shallow structures in the axial zones of the major anticlines developed in the Neogene foredeep sediments. The latter structures show a more complex structural pattern with respect to the deeper ones.
The northern Marche internal region is presently affected only by low seismic activity, but damaging earthquakes struck this area in the last two centuries (e.g. 24 April 1741, Mw 6.2 Fabrianese; 3 June 1781, Mw 6.5 Cagliese; 28 July 1799, Mw 6.2 Appennino Marchigiano, and 12 March 1873, Mw 5.9 Appennino Marchigiano). Along the line of evidence set forth in Sbarra et al. (2019), we deem that the 1781 and 1799 earthquakes have occurred at comparatively shallow depths with respect to the 1741 and 1873 events, likely occurred at deeper crustal levels.
We tentatively propose that the causative source of the deep 1741 earthquake is located on the interface between the Apennines chain in the upper plate and the Adria lithosphere in the lower plate.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Are the Northern Apennines underlain by active subduction or is present deformation taken up by major lithospheric thrusts?
2) If the active subduction exists beneath the Northern Apennines, is the magnetic basement involved in the thrusting? Therefore, is the structural style in this region thin- or thick-skinned?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Bally et al. (1986)
They propose a number of balanced cross sections at a regional scale between the Adriatic Median line and the Umbria Marche Apennines based on the integration of surface and subsurface data derived from seismic reflection profiles and wells. They propose a thin skinned tectonic mechanism: thrusts interest only the sedimentary covers and do not involve the metamorphic basement, the basal decollement is located at the base of the Burano Anidrites and thrust sheets develop over the regional monocline represented by the metamorphic basement.
Bally et al. propose these main results:
1) The position of the easternmost thrust of the Apennine system in the central Adriatic Sea;
2) The estimated shortening for the Sibillini thrust front is 35-50 km in the northern sectors; about 120 km in the southern Marche and up to 170 in the southernmost portion of the bent structure (M. Laga);
3) The presence of secondary decollement levels on marly horizons which has poor lateral continuity so that these level had to be considered secondary and localized and the associated shortening had to be added to a conservative shortening;
4) The basal decollement level deepens from the eastern sectors to the west being about 5 km depth under the Adriatic Sea and from 12 to 14 km in the Perugia region.
Barchi (1991)
In this paper Barchi suggests an alternative interpretation to the thin skinned tectonics structural style in the Umbria-Marche Apennines.
Analysing four different cross section of the Umbria Marche folded belt, all based on thin skinned tectonics over a basal decollement positioned over a regional monocline, he underlines the influence that the depth of the main decollement level has on the amount of shortening. He shows how for deeper decollement levels there is a reduction of the amount of shortening and a simplified history of deformation.
He lists the main bottom decollement levels as suggested from different authors. From the older to the younger, these decollement levels are: the bottom of the Triassic Evaporites, the Rosso Ammonitico/Marne a Fucoidi and/or the Scaglia Variegata/Cinerea formation. In a synthetic table he relates these decollement levels with the thickness of the sequence involved in the thrust sheets, with the depth of the basal detachment and with the relative amount of shortening.
Analysing a seismic reflection line (Trevi-Visso section) he proposes three alternative interpretations: 1) Section A where a single compressional event, with basal decollement at the bottom of the Triassic evaporites, produces about 170 km of shortening (70%); 2) Section B where the pre-Burano basement is involved only in two major thrusts and where two stage of deformation are assumed producing 100 km of shortening (65%); 3) In the section C all the major thrusts involve the pre-Burano sequences and the related shortening is about 74 km (57%).
Coward et al. (1999)
They integrate surface geological data with subsurface data to investigate the timing of deformation, the structural styles and the amount of deformation occurred from late Miocene to Pleistocene in the Marche-Romagna sector of the northern Apennines.
They analyse three seismic reflection profiles that highline the structural stile from the internal Mondaino ridge to the external Gabicce ridge, and reconstruct the stratigraphy of the area by exploration wells with the aims of calibrating the upper part of the seismic lines. Finally, they propose three balanced cross sections across the frontal Apennines belt and its offshore continuation in the Adriatic Sea.
The analysing of the three sections shows that: 1) the structuring of the thrust belt in this sector from late Messinian to lower Pleistocene; 2) a weak southwestward increasing in the amount of shortening; 3) a regional deformation style characterized by the presence of deep structures consisting of growth anticlines bounded by major thrust ramps, involving the Mesozoic-Paleogene carbonate succession, and of shallower structures in the crestal zones of the major anticlines affecting Neogene foredeep sediments. The last structures show a more complex structural pattern and a shorter wavelength with respect the deeper ones; 4) an important influence of basement faulting which produce a linkage of basement and cover structures giving a combination of thin and thick-skinned tectonic styles. They calculate shortening values ranging from 1.5 to 2.5 mm/yr in the late Messinian-early Pleistocene and observe a higher amount of shortening from the northern area to the southern one.
Lavecchia et al. (2002)
They use the Umbria-Marche as a case study to propose new criteria for seismotectonic zoning.
They observe that the extensional upper crustal seismicity in the Umbria-Marche Apennines is mainly confined in the hanging wall of the Altotiberina Fault (AF), a northeast dipping low angle normal fault.
From west to east they identify 6 seismotectonic zones (B1a, B2, B3, B4, B5, B1b), all these zones are characterized by extensional tectonics the eastern ones being the expression of west dipping normal faults antithetic to the AF one. It is noticeable that Lavecchia et al. consider the easternmost B1b zone the most uncertain for structural and seismotectonic role and propose that significant historical seismicity such as the 1781 Cagli earthquake might be related to immature west dipping normal faults not reaching the surface, i.e. blind normal faults, or to slip on discrete down-dip segments of the AF.
Barchi et al. (2003)
Barchi et al. offer a review of the results of the CROP 03 project.
They divide the Northern Apennines in two main different structural domains:
1) A western Tyrrhenian domain, where they observe the occurrence of positive Bouger anomalies, high values of heat flow, thinned crust with a brand new Moho (22-25 km) and an extensional regime lasting since 15 My;
2) An eastern, Adriatic domain, where gravity anomalies are negative, heat flow is low, and that is characterized by a compressional stress field started 15 My ago in the inner sectors, and still active today in the foreland zone.
They find that in the subsurface of the easternmost sector the shallow structures of the Umbria Marche thrust belt are clearly identifiable because of the presence of a triplet of reflectors with a good lateral continuity which correspond from bottom to top to: a) the top of the basement phyllites; b) the bottom of the Calcare Massiccio Fm.
(Uppermost Triassic); c) the Marne a Fucoidi Fm. (lower part of Upper Cretaceous).
Their interpretation of the CROP03 seismic line shows involvement of the shallower portion of the phyllitic basement in four major thrust faults corresponding to the main anticlinoria mapped at the surface.
They estimate a total shortening of about 60 km (30%) for the whole Umbria-Marche sector, and propose that this shortening could be transferred to the Adriatic crust or alternatively the entire Umbria-Marche thrust sheet could be completely detached from the subducting Adriatic slab.
Lavecchia et al. (2003)
The authors analyse the spatial and kinematics relationships among the deep Apennine seismicity, the upper crustal seismicity at the outer front of the Apennine thrust belt and the major crust-scale tectonic discontinuities. They propose the existence of a Plio-Quaternary SW-dipping thrust zone, named Adriatic Thrust (AT), cutting the entire Adriatic crust and emerging at the outer front of the Apennine thrust system. On the basis of active tectonics and seismicity they divide the studied sector in three main zones, from west to east these zones are: the Apennine zone, the Foothill zone and the Coastal-Adriatic zone.
In order to verify any possible seismogenic link between the AT with the shallow and deep seismicity in the Central Apennines they plot well located hypocenters of Porto S. Giorgio sequence (1987) and of the Faenza sequence (2000) along interpretative geological section. They show that the Porto S. Giorgio sequence is confined within the uppermost 6 km and it is associated with the shallower AT segment. On the contrary the Faenza hypocenters are located beneath the Romagna foothills area and are confined between 60 and 20 km of depth within the AT hanging wall. In both cases the main shocks and after shock mechanisms show reverse solutions.
They reach similar conclusions for the Reggio Emilia -Ferrara region struck by the 1983 Parma earthquake and the 1996 Reggio Emilia event.
These earthquakes present reverse solutions with a strike slip component. The Reggio Emilia main shock (Mw = 5.4) is located at 15 km depth.
In the opinion of the investigator the Po Plain -Adriatic front of the Apennine thrust system is still active, and the shallow Coastal Adriatic seismicity and the deep Apennine seismicity are kinematically compatible with an active SW-NE compression and associated with the AT lithospheric discontinuity. This interpretation implies, in their opinion, that: 1) the Po Plain-Adriatic front of the Apennine thrust system is still active; 2) the Apennines deep seismicity is not associated with a subduction plane; 3) seismogenic deformation in association with lithospheric failure is possible.
Lavecchia et al. (2004)
Re-analysing the CROP03 seismic reflection profile integrating several different dataset they confirm a thick skinned tectonic deformation style for the outer Marche region and propose a revisited geometry of the structure characterized by the presence of a SW dipping lithospheric thrust named Adriatic Thrust (AT).
They analyse the historical and instrumental seismicity of the Adriatic coast, the Marche and Romagna and of the pede-Apennine to find out the seismogenic role of the AT. Their structural model implies 45-50 km (4.0 mm/y) of shortening along the CROP03 section in the western domains, the same value proposed by Barchi et al. 1998 in their interpretation of the whole CROP03 seismic reflection profile, and lower rates of shortening 6-7 km in 2.5 My (2.5-3.0 mm/y) for the eastern domain, the Gabicce-Pesaro coastal Adriatic zone. Lavecchia et al. analyse published geodetical data (VLBI and GPS data) and consider representative of the active compression in the northern Apennines, either the value of shortening coming from Hunstad et al. 2003, 2.4 1.8 mm/y, for the southern Marche, either the rate of migration toward NE for the Romagna folds provided by Riguzzi and Zanutta, 1998 from VLBI data, 2.5 1 mm/y.
They also analysed the seismicity and focal mechanisms in the Marche inner and coastal region pointing out that the deeper ipocenter are located in the pede-Apennine sectors having compressive mechanisms that they associate to the deeper segment of the AT here located in the upper portion of the lower crust.
They conclude that the Apennines Adriatic front is the emersion of the AT that is active and seismogenic.

pictures.c: Recent seismicity plotted on geological cross sections by Lavecchia et al. [2003]. Notice the difference in depth between the Porto San Giorgio sequence, affecting the uppermost 10 km of the crust, and the Faenza sequence, occurring at 10-12 and 15-20 km depth.

pictures.t: Seismogenic zoning of the Adriatic thrust
pictures.c: The depth of the seismogenic layer varies from the inner to the outer sector of the northern Apennines. In particular, typical hypocentral depths increase from the coastal zone to the apennines crest, following the geometry of the thrusts (from Lavecchia et al. [2003]).

pictures.t: Geological cross section along seismic profiles
pictures.c: Frontal thrust faults of the northern Apennines showing deep roots in the upper crust (from Finetti et al. [2001]). The deeper seismicity in the Marche region is assumed to be generated by these faults.
Main external thrust fault that affect the whole accretionary prism of the Umbria-Marche Apennines (from Barchi et al. [1998]).
